## Simple explanation

Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measures how much one probability
distribution differs from a reference distribution. It is often used to
compare a model's predicted distribution with a target distribution.

## Technical explanation

For distributions $P$ and $Q$, the KL divergence is

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \sum_x P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}.
$$

It is not symmetric: in general, $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \neq
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)$. This makes it useful when one distribution is treated
as the reference or target and the other is an approximation to it.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

KL divergence appears in variational inference, model compression, and
loss functions such as cross-entropy. It quantifies mismatch between
predicted and target distributions, and it underlies several training and
evaluation objectives.

## How it works

The divergence is large when the model assigns probability mass to events that
are unlikely under the reference distribution. It is zero only when the two
distributions are identical where $P$ has support. In practice, smoothing and
numerical care are important when probabilities are close to zero.

## Practical example

A model predicts a probability distribution over next-token options. If its
predicted distribution differs substantially from the true distribution of the
ground-truth label, KL divergence becomes large. It can be used as part of a
training objective or for evaluation.

## Common misconceptions

- KL divergence is not a distance metric because it is asymmetric.
- A small KL value does not necessarily mean the distributions look similar to a human observer in every way.
- It is not defined in all cases without careful handling of zeros and support.
